lines.text: This chapter shifted us from the crisp world of pure polarization into the messier reality of flop and turn play, where most bets are hybrids of fold equity and pot equity.
We saw that protection is not about beating strong draws; it is about denying free cards to hands with a few live outs and little other way to win.
We introduced linear ranges as the natural shape for raise-or-fold spots, all-in bluffs, and small-bet strategies.
We saw how solvers construct elaborate multi-size strategies that only marginally beat simpler human-executable ones, and how you should default to the simpler play in almost every real spot.
And we saw how a big equity advantage lets you push equity with small bets, extracting value from your whole range while making raises unattractive for your opponent.
The one habit to keep from this chapter is asking, before every flop decision: which shape does my range want to be here, polarized, condensed, or linear?
That question alone gets you three-quarters of the way to the right strategy in most spots.
In the next chapter, we will make range construction itself the object of study, walking through the mechanics of building a betting range and a defending range one hand at a time.
